Replace the doc comment, signature and opening of `search_and_enumerate`, and the single test line that follows its `Searched` struct's use. The function, currently

```rust
    /// Plans `q` under `policy` and enumerates every order the column-order
    /// constraints allow. `None` when `stored` finds `q` cyclic.
    fn search_and_enumerate(
        q: &JoinQuery, relations: &Relations, policy: ColumnOrderPolicy,
    ) -> Option<Searched> {
        if policy == ColumnOrderPolicy::Stored && check_attribute_order(q).is_err() {
            return None;
        }
        let relations: Vec<(&str, usize, &[usize])> = relations
            .iter()
            .map(|(name, tuples, distinct)| (name.as_str(), *tuples, distinct.as_slice()))
            .collect();
        let stats = stats_under(q, policy, &relations);
        let analysis = analyse(q);
        let model = CostModel::new(q, &analysis.predicate_variables, analysis.num_vars, &stats);
        let predecessors = Precedence::for_query(q, &stats)
            .predecessor_masks()
            .unwrap();
        let mut best: Option<(f64, Vec<usize>)> = None;
        for order in valid_orders(&predecessors) {
            let cost = cost_of(&model, &order);
            if best.as_ref().is_none_or(|(least, _)| cost < *least) {
                best = Some((cost, order));
            }
        }
        let (least, cheapest) = best.expect("an acyclic query has a valid order");
        let plan = CostBasedOptimiser::default()
            .plan(q, &stats)
            .variable_ordering;
        Some(Searched {
            plan_cost: cost_of(&model, &plan),
            plan,
            cheapest,
            least,
        })
    }

    /// Plans `q` and enumerates every order of its variables.
    fn search_and_enumerate(q: &JoinQuery, relations: &Relations) -> Searched {
        let relations: Vec<(&str, usize, &[usize])> = relations
            .iter()
            .map(|(name, tuples, distinct)| (name.as_str(), *tuples, distinct.as_slice()))
            .collect();
        let stats = stats_for(q, &relations);
        let analysis = analyse(q);
        let model = CostModel::new(q, &analysis.predicate_variables, analysis.num_vars, &stats);
        let predecessors = Precedence::free(analysis.num_vars)
            .predecessor_masks()
            .unwrap();
        let mut best: Option<(f64, Vec<usize>)> = None;
        for order in valid_orders(&predecessors) {
            let cost = cost_of(&model, &order);
            if best.as_ref().is_none_or(|(least, _)| cost < *least) {
                best = Some((cost, order));
            }
        }
        let (least, cheapest) = best.expect("every query has an order");

            .plan(q, &stats)
            .variable_ordering;

            plan_cost: cost_of(&model, &plan),
            plan,
            cheapest,
            least,
        }

    /// The search is exact for its cost model: on random queries whose
    /// statistics span orders of magnitude, under both policies, its plan
    /// costs what the cheapest order the column-order constraints allow
    /// does, as brute force over every valid order finds it. Exactly,
    /// although `f64` rounds: the search sums each order's estimates in the
    /// order `cost_of` does, and rounding is monotonic, so no order can come
    /// out cheaper than the plan. And `any`, which allows every order
    /// `stored` does, never plans dearer.
    #[test]
    #[cfg_attr(
        miri,
        ignore = "enumerates every valid order, minutes under Miri; the tests above run the \
                  search there"
    )]
    fn the_search_finds_the_cheapest_valid_order() {
        // Cases searched under `stored` (the rest are cyclic there), and
        // cases where `any` found a strictly cheaper plan.
        let (mut stored_cases, mut any_cheaper) = (0, 0);
        for seed in 0..SEARCH_SEEDS {
            let (text, relations) = random_case(&mut Lcg(seed), Counts::Wide);
            let q: JoinQuery = text.parse().unwrap();
            let mut least = Vec::new();
            for policy in [ColumnOrderPolicy::Stored, ColumnOrderPolicy::Any] {
                let Some(searched) = search_and_enumerate(&q, &relations, policy) else {
                    continue;
                };
                assert_eq!(
                    searched.plan_cost, searched.least,
                    "seed {seed}, {policy:?}: {text}: planned {:?}, cheapest {:?}",
                    searched.plan, searched.cheapest
                );
                least.push(searched.least);
            }
            if let [stored, any] = least[..] {
                assert!(any <= stored, "seed {seed}: {text}");
                stored_cases += 1;
                any_cheaper += usize::from(any < stored);
            }
        }
        // The first 300 seeds give 249 queries `stored` can plan (the other
        // 51 are cyclic there), 136 of which `any` plans cheaper. The bounds
        // catch a generator that stops producing cases where the policies
        // differ.
        assert!(
            stored_cases >= 200 && any_cheaper >= 80,
            "stored {stored_cases}, any cheaper {any_cheaper}"
        );
    }

    /// Among plans of equal cost the search takes the lexicographically
    /// smallest order, as brute force does, on random queries whose
    /// statistics make ties common and exact.
    #[test]
    #[cfg_attr(
        miri,
        ignore = "enumerates every valid order, minutes under Miri; the tests above run the \
                  search there"
    )]
    fn random_ties_take_the_lexicographically_smaller_order() {
        for seed in 0..SEARCH_SEEDS {
            let (text, relations) = random_case(&mut Lcg(seed), Counts::SmallPowersOfTwo);
            let q: JoinQuery = text.parse().unwrap();
            for policy in [ColumnOrderPolicy::Stored, ColumnOrderPolicy::Any] {
                if let Some(searched) = search_and_enumerate(&q, &relations, policy) {
                    assert_eq!(
                        searched.plan, searched.cheapest,
                        "seed {seed}, {policy:?}: {text}"
                    );
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

```rust
//! Variable ordering shared by all optimisers.

use std::{
    cmp::Reverse,
    collections::{BinaryHeap, HashSet},
};

/// Computes a *global attribute order* (GAO): a permutation of the query's
/// variables in which every edge of `precedence` points forward.
///
/// A query builds each of its indexes with the columns in plan order, so no
/// relation's stored column order constrains the plan. [`Precedence::free`],
/// the graph every optimiser plans under, has no edge, and every
/// permutation is valid. Kahn's algorithm yields a valid order for any
/// acyclic graph.
///
/// `rank` maps a candidate variable to an [`Ord`] key; among the variables
/// whose predecessors are all emitted (the *ready set*), the smallest key is
/// emitted next, with the canonical index as the final deterministic
/// tie-break. Because candidates are restricted to the ready set, **any**
/// rank function yields a valid order — an ordering policy can be slow,
/// never wrong. `rank` is evaluated once per variable, as it becomes ready
/// — cheap enough for expensive statistics-driven policies.
///
/// # Panics
///
/// Panics if the edges are cyclic, which no graph the optimisers build is.
pub fn topological_order<K: Ord>(precedence: &Precedence, rank: impl Fn(usize) -> K) -> Vec<usize> {
    let order = precedence.kahn(rank);
    assert_eq!(
        order.len(),
        precedence.num_vars(),
        "precedence edges are cyclic; no variable order satisfies them"
    );
    order
}

/// The ordering-constraint graph: an edge `u -> v` requires `u` bound before
/// `v`. Every optimiser plans under [`Precedence::free`], which has none.
/// The edge machinery stays because [`topological_order`] orders by it and
/// the cost-based search reads its
/// [`predecessor_masks`](Self::predecessor_masks), so neither can disagree
/// about which plans are valid.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct Precedence {
    /// `adjacency[v]`: the variables that must be bound after `v`.
    adjacency: Vec<HashSet<usize>>,
    /// Number of distinct variables that must be bound before each one.
    in_degree: Vec<usize>,
}

impl Precedence {
    /// The graph over `num_vars` variables with no edge: every order is
    /// valid, and the ranking alone decides.
    pub fn free(num_vars: usize) -> Self {
        Self {
            adjacency: vec![HashSet::new(); num_vars],
            in_degree: vec![0; num_vars],
        }
    }

    /// The graph with one edge `col[i] -> col[i+1]` per adjacent pair of
    /// each atom's variables, a variable repeated within one atom imposing
    /// no self-constraint. The shape a stored column order used to impose;
    /// kept for the tests that exercise Kahn's algorithm with edges.
    #[cfg(test)]
    fn with_edges(num_vars: usize, predicate_variables: &[Vec<usize>]) -> Self {
        let mut precedence = Self::free(num_vars);
        for vars in predicate_variables {
            for pair in vars.windows(2) {
                let (earlier, later) = (pair[0], pair[1]);
                if earlier != later && precedence.adjacency[earlier].insert(later) {
                    precedence.in_degree[later] += 1;
                }
            }
        }
        precedence
    }

    /// The number of variables the graph orders.
    pub fn num_vars(&self) -> usize { self.in_degree.len() }

    /// Whether the graph has no edge at all, so every order is valid.
    pub fn is_free(&self) -> bool { self.in_degree.iter().all(|&d| d == 0) }

    /// The variables each variable must follow, as one bitmask per variable:
    /// bit `u` of entry `v` is set when `u -> v` is an edge. A set of bound
    /// variables `S` can bind `v` next exactly when `masks[v] & !S == 0`.
    /// `None` past 64 variables, which a `u64` cannot index.
    pub fn predecessor_masks(&self) -> Option<Vec<u64>> {
        let num_vars = self.num_vars();
        if num_vars > 64 {
            return None;
        }
        let mut masks = vec![0u64; num_vars];
        for (earlier, laters) in self.adjacency.iter().enumerate() {
            for &later in laters {
                masks[later] |= 1u64 << earlier;
            }
        }
        Some(masks)
    }

    /// Kahn's algorithm, emitting the smallest-`rank` ready variable first.
    /// The result is shorter than `num_vars` exactly when the constraints
    /// are cyclic: the variables on and after a cycle never become ready.
    fn kahn<K: Ord>(&self, rank: impl Fn(usize) -> K) -> Vec<usize> {
        let num_vars = self.in_degree.len();
        let mut in_degree = self.in_degree.clone();
        let mut ready: BinaryHeap<Reverse<(K, usize)>> = (0..num_vars)
            .filter(|&v| in_degree[v] == 0)
            .map(|v| Reverse((rank(v), v)))
            .collect();
        let mut order = Vec::with_capacity(num_vars);
        while let Some(Reverse((_, v))) = ready.pop() {
            order.push(v);
            for &w in &self.adjacency[v] {
                in_degree[w] -= 1;
                if in_degree[w] == 0 {
                    ready.push(Reverse((rank(w), w)));
                }
            }
        }
        order
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn a_free_graph_orders_by_rank_with_the_canonical_index_as_tie_break() {
        let free = Precedence::free(3);
        assert!(free.is_free());
        assert_eq!(free.num_vars(), 3);
        assert_eq!(topological_order(&free, |v| v), vec![0, 1, 2]);
        // The rank alone decides.
        assert_eq!(topological_order(&free, |v| 2 - v), vec![2, 1, 0]);
        // Equal ranks fall back to the canonical index.
        assert_eq!(topological_order(&free, |_| 0), vec![0, 1, 2]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_free_graph_has_no_predecessors() {
        assert_eq!(Precedence::free(3).predecessor_masks().unwrap(), vec![
            0, 0, 0
        ]);
        assert_eq!(
            topological_order(&Precedence::free(0), |v| v),
            Vec::<usize>::new()
        );
    }

    #[test]
    fn identity_rank_reproduces_lexicographic_order() {
        // Triangle: R(0,1), S(1,2), T(0,2) — edges 0->1, 1->2, 0->2.
        let preds = vec![vec![0, 1], vec![1, 2], vec![0, 2]];
        let graph = Precedence::with_edges(3, &preds);
        assert!(!graph.is_free());
        assert_eq!(topological_order(&graph, |v| v), vec![0, 1, 2]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn an_edge_forces_a_late_canonical_variable_first() {
        // r(K, Y) with K canonical index 1, Y index 0: edge 1 -> 0.
        let preds = vec![vec![1, 0], vec![1]];
        assert_eq!(
            topological_order(&Precedence::with_edges(2, &preds), |v| v),
            vec![1, 0]
        );
    }

    #[test]
    fn rank_breaks_ties_among_ready_variables() {
        // Star: R(0,1), S(0,2). After 0, both 1 and 2 are ready; the rank
        // function prefers 2.
        let preds = vec![vec![0, 1], vec![0, 2]];
        let order = topological_order(&Precedence::with_edges(3, &preds), |v| {
            if v == 2 {
                0
            } else {
                v + 1
            }
        });
        assert_eq!(order, vec![0, 2, 1]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn predecessor_masks_mirror_the_edges() {
        // Triangle: R(0,1), S(1,2), T(0,2) — edges 0->1, 1->2, 0->2.
        let preds = vec![vec![0, 1], vec![1, 2], vec![0, 2]];
        let masks = Precedence::with_edges(3, &preds)
            .predecessor_masks()
            .unwrap();
        assert_eq!(masks, vec![0b000, 0b001, 0b011]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn predecessor_masks_stop_at_64_variables() {
        assert!(Precedence::free(65).predecessor_masks().is_none());
        let masks = Precedence::free(64).predecessor_masks().unwrap();
        assert_eq!(masks.len(), 64);
    }

    #[test]
    #[should_panic(expected = "precedence edges are cyclic")]
    fn cyclic_edges_panic() {
        // r(X, Y), s(Y, X): edges 0->1 and 1->0.
        let preds = vec![vec![0, 1], vec![1, 0]];
        topological_order(&Precedence::with_edges(2, &preds), |v| v);
    }
}

```rust
//! The default ordering policy: smallest canonical variable index first.

use crate::optimiser::{
    ordering::{topological_order, Precedence},
    CatalogStats, QueryOptimiser, QueryPlan,
};

/// Plans the global attribute order by Kahn's topological sort with a
/// smallest-canonical-index tie-break.
///
/// This reproduces, bit for bit, the ordering kermit hardcoded before
/// query optimisers existed — it keeps head variables early when
/// unconstrained and is fully deterministic. It ignores statistics, which
/// makes it the control arm for optimiser ablation studies and the
/// default everywhere. Under `--column-orders any` nothing constrains it,
/// so the plan is the canonical order itself.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, Default, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct LexicographicOptimiser;

impl QueryOptimiser for LexicographicOptimiser {
    fn plan(&self, query: &kermit_parser::JoinQuery, stats: &CatalogStats) -> QueryPlan {
        QueryPlan {
            variable_ordering: topological_order(&Precedence::for_query(query, stats), |v| v),
        }
    }
}

**`planner.rs`.** Replace everything above `#[cfg(test)]` with:

```rust
//! The planner: the optimiser a query is planned with.

use {
    super::{CatalogStats, QueryOptimiser, QueryPlan, StatisticsLevel},
    kermit_parser::JoinQuery,
    std::fmt,
};

/// What plans a join: a [`QueryOptimiser`].
///
/// The join entry points (`kermit::db`), the CLI's families and the test
/// harness all pass one of these where they used to pass a bare
/// `&dyn QueryOptimiser`. `kermit::db::prepare` plans a query once, before
/// anything is timed. No column order constrains the plan, since an index is
/// built with its columns in plan order, so a planner is its optimiser and
/// nothing else.
pub struct Planner {
    optimiser: Box<dyn QueryOptimiser>,
}

impl Planner {
    /// A planner running `optimiser`.
    pub fn new(optimiser: Box<dyn QueryOptimiser>) -> Self {
        Self {
            optimiser,
        }
    }

    /// The statistics the optimiser reads
    /// ([`QueryOptimiser::required_statistics`]).
    pub fn required_statistics(&self) -> StatisticsLevel { self.optimiser.required_statistics() }

    /// Plans `query` from `stats` ([`QueryOptimiser::plan`]).
    pub fn plan(&self, query: &JoinQuery, stats: &CatalogStats) -> QueryPlan {
        self.optimiser.plan(query, stats)
    }
}

impl fmt::Debug for Planner {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        f.debug_struct("Planner")
            .field("required_statistics", &self.required_statistics())
            .finish_non_exhaustive()
    }
}

```

/// Per-relation statistics for the predicates of one query, plus the
/// column-order policy the plan is made under.
///
/// Plain data: planners never touch data structures, so they stay
/// data-structure-agnostic and unit-testable with literal maps. Callers
/// build one per join via [`CatalogStats::for_query`]. The policy rides
/// along because it decides which atoms *pin* the plan to their stored
/// column order ([`is_pinned`](Self::is_pinned)); no optimiser reads that
/// any more, and Task 23.2 deletes the policy.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Default, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct CatalogStats {
    relations: BTreeMap<String, RelationStats>,
    column_orders: ColumnOrderPolicy,
}
```

with

```rust
/// Per-relation statistics for the predicates of one query.
///
/// Plain data: planners never touch data structures, so they stay
/// data-structure-agnostic and unit-testable with literal maps. Callers
/// build one per query via [`CatalogStats::for_query`].
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Default, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct CatalogStats {
    relations: BTreeMap<String, RelationStats>,

```

Replace `for_query` and the two methods after it, from the doc comment `/// Builds stats for every body predicate of `query`, under` through the end of `is_pinned`, currently

```rust
    /// Builds stats for every body predicate of `query`, under
    /// `column_orders`.
    ///
    /// `stats_of` supplies a predicate's statistics (in `kermit::db`, those
    /// of the access the predicate names, which it counts through the
    /// access's filter). Predicates the lookup does not know get no entry
    /// — planners treat missing stats as "assume large".
    pub fn for_query(
        query: &JoinQuery, column_orders: ColumnOrderPolicy,
        stats_of: impl Fn(&str) -> Option<RelationStats>,
    ) -> Self {
        let mut stats = CatalogStats {
            column_orders,
            ..CatalogStats::default()
        };
        for pred in &query.body {
            if stats.relations.contains_key(&pred.name) {
                continue;
            }
            if let Some(relation) = stats_of(&pred.name) {
                stats.insert(pred.name.clone(), relation);
            }
        }
        stats
    }

    /// The column-order policy these statistics were built under.
    pub fn column_orders(&self) -> ColumnOrderPolicy { self.column_orders }

    /// Whether the atom named `name` must bind its columns left to right,
    /// i.e. adds its column-order edges to the plan's precedence graph.
    ///
    /// `stored` pins every relation and `any` pins none, so today the
    /// name is not consulted; it is the seam for a selective policy
    /// (issue #82: a relation with a stored reordered copy is free). A
    /// `Select_<n>_<base>` view follows its base, and a `Const_*`
    /// singleton is unary, so pinning it changes nothing.
    pub fn is_pinned(&self, _name: &str) -> bool {
        match self.column_orders {
            | ColumnOrderPolicy::Stored => true,
            | ColumnOrderPolicy::Any => false,
        }
    }
}
```

    pub fn for_query(

**`mod.rs`.** Replace the module doc, currently

```rust
//! Query optimisers: planners that choose the global attribute order.
//!
//! Kermit separates planning from execution. A [`QueryOptimiser`] consumes
//! a parsed, rewritten (const, placeholder, selection) [`JoinQuery`] plus
//! per-relation statistics
//! ([`CatalogStats`]) and produces a [`QueryPlan`]. A [`Planner`] bundles
//! an optimiser with the [`ColumnOrderPolicy`] it plans under;
//! `kermit::db` passes one where it used to pass a bare optimiser. Join
//! algorithms (`JoinAlgo::join_for_each`) execute the plan. The space of
//! valid plans is
//! exactly the set of topological orders of the column-order constraint
//! DAG (see [`topological_order`]); the provided optimisers are valid by
//! construction, and executors defensively assert
//! [`QueryPlan::validate`].
```

with

```rust
//! Query optimisers: planners that choose the global attribute order.
//!
//! Kermit separates planning from execution. A [`QueryOptimiser`] consumes
//! a query of accesses (see `kermit_algos::extract_accesses`) plus
//! per-relation statistics ([`CatalogStats`]) and produces a [`QueryPlan`].
//! A [`Planner`] holds an optimiser; `kermit::db` passes one where it used
//! to pass a bare optimiser. Join algorithms (`JoinAlgo::join_for_each`)
//! execute the plan. Every permutation of the variables is a valid plan,
//! since each index is built with its columns in plan order (see
//! [`topological_order`] and [`Precedence::free`]); executors defensively
//! assert [`QueryPlan::validate`].
```

```rust
/// Implementations receive the query *after* the const, placeholder and
/// selection rewrites (the exact query the executor will run, including
/// synthetic `Const_*` and `Select_*` predicates) and produce a [`QueryPlan`]
/// the executor consumes. Object safe: the engine holds `Box<dyn
/// QueryOptimiser>` so the choice is a runtime decision. The returned plan must
/// order variables consistently with every relation's physical column order
/// (any [`topological_order`] output qualifies); executors assert
/// [`QueryPlan::validate`] and panic on violation.
```

with

```rust

/// `Box<dyn QueryOptimiser>` so the choice is a runtime decision. The
/// returned plan orders the query's variables (any [`topological_order`]
/// output over [`Precedence::free`] qualifies); executors assert

```

//! in the relation's column order. A subject-position constant used to
//! introduce a fresh variable that is physically first but appears late,
//! inverting that order and silently yielding 0 results. Now the constant is
//! a filter on the index and the index's columns follow the plan, so a plan
//! may bind `X` wherever it likes.
//!
//! Each case runs under every optimiser: the shape exists to guard descent
//! order, and each optimiser orders it differently.
```

In the `kermit_algos::{…}` import list, delete `ColumnOrderPolicy,`. Replace everything from the doc comment `/// `query` over edge = {(1,2), (1,3), (2,4)} as `R` through `JA`, planned` to the end of the file with:

```rust
/// `query` over edge = {(1,2), (1,3), (2,4)} as `R` through `JA`, planned
/// by `optimiser`: the rows, and the index specs the query built.
fn join_with_specs<R: Relation + Cardinality, JA: JoinEntry<R>>(
    query: &str, optimiser: Optimiser,
) -> (Vec<Vec<usize>>, Vec<IndexSpec>) {
    let planner = Planner::new(optimiser.instantiate());
    let header = RelationHeader::new_positional("edge", 2);
    let inputs: Inputs = BTreeMap::from([("edge".to_string(), (header, Tuples::from(edges())))]);
    let catalog = catalog_of(&inputs, planner.required_statistics());
    let q: JoinQuery = query.parse().expect("parse");
    join_under_planner::<R, JA>(&catalog, q, &planner).unwrap()
}

/// The rows of [`join_with_specs`].
fn join<R: Relation + Cardinality, JA: JoinEntry<R>>(
    query: &str, optimiser: Optimiser,
) -> Vec<Vec<usize>> {
    join_with_specs::<R, JA>(query, optimiser).0
}

/// `query` as a `TreeTrie` (LFTJ path).
fn lftj(query: &str, optimiser: Optimiser) -> Vec<Vec<usize>> {
    join::<TreeTrie, LeapfrogTriejoin>(query, optimiser)
}

/// The same over a `HashTrie` (hash path).
fn hash(query: &str, optimiser: Optimiser) -> Vec<Vec<usize>> {
    join::<HashTrieSip, HashTriejoin>(query, optimiser)
}

/// First column (the head variable `X`) of every result tuple, sorted.
fn head_col(mut rows: Vec<Vec<usize>>) -> Vec<usize> {
    let mut out: Vec<usize> = rows.iter_mut().map(|r| r[0]).collect();
    out.sort_unstable();
    out
}

// Q(X) :- edge(c1, X).  — successors of node 1 are {2, 3}.
#[test]
fn subject_position_constant_lftj() {
    for &optimiser in Optimiser::value_variants() {
        let got = head_col(lftj("Q(X) :- edge(c1, X).", optimiser));
        assert_eq!(got, vec![2, 3], "{optimiser:?}");
    }
}

#[test]
fn subject_position_constant_hash() {
    for &optimiser in Optimiser::value_variants() {
        let got = head_col(hash("Q(X) :- edge(c1, X).", optimiser));
        assert_eq!(got, vec![2, 3], "{optimiser:?}");
    }
}

// Q(X) :- edge(X, c4).  — predecessors of node 4 are {2}. Control case:
// object-position constants already worked; pin that they still do.
#[test]
fn object_position_constant_lftj() {
    for &optimiser in Optimiser::value_variants() {
        let got = head_col(lftj("Q(X) :- edge(X, c4).", optimiser));
        assert_eq!(got, vec![2], "{optimiser:?}");
    }
}

#[test]
fn object_position_constant_hash() {
    for &optimiser in Optimiser::value_variants() {
        let got = head_col(hash("Q(X) :- edge(X, c4).", optimiser));
        assert_eq!(got, vec![2], "{optimiser:?}");
    }
}

/// A constant or a repeated variable is not a relation to join: `prepare`
/// pushes it into the filter of the one index its atom reads, which keeps
/// only the columns that bind a variable. Each query binds one variable of
/// `edge`, so the index has one column whatever order a plan prefers.
#[test]
fn constants_and_repeats_become_the_filter_of_the_index_an_atom_reads() {
    let cases = [
        (
            "Q(X) :- edge(c1, X).",
            Filter::new(vec![(0, 1)], vec![]),
            vec![1],
        ),
        (
            "Q(X) :- edge(X, c4).",
            Filter::new(vec![(1, 4)], vec![]),
            vec![0],
        ),
        (
            "Q(X) :- edge(X, X).",
            Filter::new(vec![], vec![(0, 1)]),
            vec![0],
        ),
    ];
    for &optimiser in Optimiser::value_variants() {
        for (query, filter, columns) in &cases {
            let want = vec![IndexSpec {
                relation: "edge".to_string(),
                filter: filter.clone(),
                columns: columns.clone(),
            }];
            let (_, lftj) = join_with_specs::<TreeTrie, LeapfrogTriejoin>(query, optimiser);
            assert_eq!(lftj, want, "LFTJ {query}: {optimiser:?}");
            let (_, hash) = join_with_specs::<HashTrieSip, HashTriejoin>(query, optimiser);
            assert_eq!(hash, want, "HTJ {query}: {optimiser:?}");
        }
    }
}
```

## Story 24: Report schema v5 and kermit-lab

- **Developer:** intermediate-dev
- **Files:** `kermit/src/bench_report.rs`, `kermit/tests/cli_join_tests.rs`, `python/kermit-lab/kermit_lab/__init__.py`, `python/kermit-lab/kermit_lab/loader.py`, `python/kermit-lab/kermit_lab/defaults.py`, `python/kermit-lab/kermit_lab/frame.py`, `python/kermit-lab/kermit_lab/presets.py`, `python/kermit-lab/kermit_lab/analysis.py`, `python/kermit-lab/kermit_lab/drivers/main.py`, `python/kermit-lab/kermit_lab/drivers/render_all.py`, `python/kermit-lab/README.md`, `python/kermit-lab/tests/test_loader.py`, `python/kermit-lab/tests/test_cli.py`, `python/kermit-lab/tests/test_frame.py`, `python/kermit-lab/tests/test_defaults.py`, `python/kermit-lab/tests/conftest.py`, `python/kermit-lab/tests/test_presets.py`, `python/kermit-lab/tests/test_analysis.py`, `python/kermit-lab/tests/test_contract.py`, `python/kermit-lab/notebooks/07_lubm_reference_comparison.ipynb`
- **Interfaces:** uses the report keys of Stories 16–17; sets `SCHEMA_VERSION = 5` for the final gate's contract test
- **Verify:** `cargo test -p kermit --bin kermit bench_report`
- **Review:** deep

`REPORT_SCHEMA_VERSION` becomes 5 with a history entry, and kermit-lab follows Amendment 1 §10: `SCHEMA_VERSION` and `PER_QUERY_BUILD_SCHEMA` are 5 with a v5 `MEANING_CHANGES` entry, `TIME_PHASES` gains `build` (so v4 and earlier reports still load on their own), the three default phases that were `insertion` become `build`, the `column_orders` back-fill stops at v5, and the README, the pytest suite and the real-binary contract test move to v5. Two further changes are drafted here. First, `python/kermit-lab/kermit_lab/frame.py` changes: the back-fill can only be limited to rows older than v5 if the frame knows each row's `schema_version`, so the frame gains a `schema_version` column, and it gains `index_rows` (the new v5 axis, otherwise silently dropped by the include-list). Second, a v5 fixture and a `schema_version` parameter on `conftest._write_report`. A third, small one: the `phase` docstring of `drivers/render_all.py` names the build phase for v5 reports. A fourth: notebook 07 runs `bench run` with `--metrics insertion` and plots `phase="insertion"` for the reports that run produces, which stops parsing after Story 16; Task 24.6 moves both to `build`. Notebooks 06 and 00 plot existing pre-v5 reports and stay. No landmine marker is in this story's code. Task 24.1 lands the Rust constant and kermit-lab's `SCHEMA_VERSION` together, because `python_schema_version_matches_rust` pins them; every task leaves the pytest suite green (the contract test is skipped without `KERMIT_BIN`).

def test_column_orders_backfill_stops_at_schema_v5() -> None:
    """The `stored` fill is ground truth for a report before #93 and false for a
    v5 report, which has no such axis."""
    df = pd.DataFrame({

    assert out["column_orders"].iloc[1] == "stored"
    assert pd.isna(out["column_orders"].iloc[2])
    assert pd.isna(out["column_orders"].iloc[3])

def test_column_orders_backfill_treats_an_unknown_schema_as_legacy() -> None:

`kermit-lab` parses `BenchReport` JSON up to v4 (see
```

```
`kermit-lab` parses `BenchReport` JSON up to v5 (see
`docs/specs/bench-report-schema.md`). The loader refuses to parse unknown
major versions. It also refuses to mix reports from both sides of v3, of v4,
or of v5 in one load: at v3 `iteration` and `end_to_end` changed meaning, at
v4 `insertion`, `copies`, `end_to_end`, HashTrie's `space` and
lazy-expansion HashTrie's `iteration` did (#111), and at v5 each query builds,
and times, only the indexes it reads: `build` replaces `insertion` and
`copies`, and `iteration`, `end_to_end` and `space` are measured per query, so
no metric is comparable across v4 and v5. Pass
`allow_mixed_schema=True` to `kl.load` / `kl.load_samples` to override, for
example to compare `space` across v3. Fixed axis columns (`data_structure`, `algorithm`, `query`,
`tuples`, etc.) are listed in `kermit_lab/frame.py`; optimization axes
(`ds_layout_*`, `ds_config_*`, `ds_build_mode`) are discovered dynamically
from the reports and added as additional DataFrame columns. Use
`kl.discover_opt_columns(df)` to enumerate them. `verified` (nullable
boolean) is present when `bench run --verify` checked the query's answer
count. Every row carries its report's `schema_version`. A v5 report adds
`index_rows`, the rows the query's builds copied, and has no `column_orders`
axis: the `column_orders: stored` back-fill applies only to join rows of
reports older than v5, since a v5 report never ran that policy.
```

### Task 25.1: CLAUDE.md, the Workspace Architecture and Key Trait Hierarchy sections

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement**

Run the script below from the repository root by wrapping it as `python3 -I - CLAUDE.md <<'PYEOF'` ... `PYEOF` (the script reads the file named on the command line). Each `sub` quotes the exact old text it replaces; each `line` replaces the one whole line that starts with the quoted prefix.

```python
import sys

path = sys.argv[1]
with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    text = handle.read()


def sub(old, new):
    global text
    found = text.count(old)
    assert found == 1, f"expected one match, found {found}: {old[:70]!r}"
    text = text.replace(old, new)


def line(prefix, new):
    """Replace the one line that starts with `prefix`; `new` None deletes it."""
    global text
    lines = text.split("\n")
    hits = [i for i, current in enumerate(lines) if current.startswith(prefix)]
    assert len(hits) == 1, f"expected one line, found {len(hits)}: {prefix!r}"
    if new is None:
        del lines[hits[0]]
    else:
        lines[hits[0]] = new
    text = "\n".join(lines)


# --- Workspace Architecture ---------------------------------------------------------------
sub(
    r'''kermit-iters    → Core iterator traits (LinearIterator, TrieIterator) and the tuple batch
                  (Tuples, RowId, LeafRows, ChainLinks; #111, #101). Zero dependencies.''',
    r'''kermit-iters    → Core iterator traits (LinearIterator, TrieIterator), the tuple batch
                  (Tuples, RowId, LeafRows, ChainLinks; #111, #101) and the borrowed view
                  every index is built from (TupleView, Filter). Zero dependencies.''',
)
sub(
    r'''                  are generic over a SeekStrategy Layout (seek.rs). morsel.rs holds the
                  morsel-driven partition and build steps of the parallel builds.''',
    r'''                  are generic over a SeekStrategy Layout (seek.rs). Every structure is built
                  from a borrowed TupleView (Relation::from_view) and copies its rows once.
                  morsel.rs holds the morsel-driven partition and build steps of the parallel
                  builds, which read views too.''',
)
sub(
    r'''                  JoinAlgo::join_for_each executes, bundled with a ColumnOrderPolicy in a
                  Planner; and `orient`, the orientation rewrite that reads an atom whose
                  plan disagrees with its stored column order through a reordered copy.''',
    r'''                  JoinAlgo::join_for_each executes, held by a Planner. It also hosts the two
                  steps around planning: `access`, which rewrites a query into one Access per
                  atom (relation, Filter, kept columns), and `index_plan`, which turns the
                  plan into the IndexSpecs (relation, Filter, column order) a query builds.''',
)
sub(
    r'''                  db::lftj_join / db::hash_join collect through them,
                  over a `db::Database<R>` (relations plus the planner statistics
                  gathered when it is built); all return
                  `Result<_, db::JoinError>` after db::validate_query's checks.''',
    r'''                  db::lftj_join / db::hash_join collect through them. Each runs the
                  per-query lifecycle over a `db::Catalog` (flat Tuples plus statistics;
                  no structure is built at load): `db::prepare` (validate, plan, name the
                  indexes; untimed), `db::build` (one index per IndexSpec, each built
                  from a TupleView; timed) and `db::execute` (the join; timed). All
                  return `Result<_, db::JoinError>` after db::validate_query's checks.''',
)

# --- Key Trait Hierarchy --------------------------------------------------------------------
sub(
    r'''sharing one body via the `JoinFamily` trait)''',
    r'''both over the one `prepare` / `build` / `execute` lifecycle)''',
)

On a family whose joins mutate their relations (`ExecutionFamily::JOIN_MUTATES`, a lazy HashTrie) the fresh indexes `--verify` and `iteration` run on are built the same way, and `space` checks the built indexes are as built. An index's header holds the relation's kept attributes in output order; `kermit::db`'s lifecycle builds it from the spec and the base relation's header (a private helper, since `kermit-algos` cannot name `RelationHeader`).''',

A zero count means no answers; otherwise the counts multiply into `Indexes::multiplicity()`, each clamped to 1 unless `R::KEEPS_DUPLICATES` (`HashTrie` counts duplicate rows, the sorted tries do not). `execute` emits each row `multiplicity` times, and when every atom was a check it emits the empty head row `multiplicity` times without calling the join (the head is empty, since validation requires every head variable to be bound in the body).''',

Per query, `bench run` and `bench join` emit the Criterion functions `build` (`iter_batched` with a no-op setup and `BatchSize::PerIteration`), `iteration` (`execute` over indexes built once outside Criterion; a fresh build per sample under `JOIN_MUTATES`; planning excluded), `end_to_end` (`build` plus K × `execute`, K = `--queries-per-build`) and `space` (the query's indexes together); `bench ds` emits `{ds}/build`, `{ds}/iteration`, `{ds}/end_to_end` and `{ds}/space`. Freeing what a timed step built is never timed: each step returns its indexes and Criterion drops them after the timer stops. `--metrics` takes `build`, `iteration`, `space` (the default) and the opt-in `end-to-end`; `insertion` and `copies` are gone. There is no `--column-orders`, so two runs under one `--name` differ only by `--optimiser`, which the Criterion group omits: give each its own `--name`.''',
)

It rewrites the whole span from `### Query validation` to the `## Benchmarking` heading in one step, so the section list reads in pipeline order (validation, placeholders, access extraction, head projection, planning, index planning). Headings sit inside Python strings with no leading `#`, which is why they are written as separate list items.

```python
import sys

path = sys.argv[1]
with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    text = handle.read()


def sub(old, new):
    global text
    found = text.count(old)
    assert found == 1, f"expected one match, found {found}: {old[:70]!r}"
    text = text.replace(old, new)


def line(prefix, new):
    """Replace the one line that starts with `prefix`; `new` None deletes it."""
    global text
    lines = text.split("\n")
    hits = [i for i, current in enumerate(lines) if current.startswith(prefix)]
    assert len(hits) == 1, f"expected one line, found {len(hits)}: {prefix!r}"
    if new is None:
        del lines[hits[0]]
    else:
        lines[hits[0]] = new
    text = "\n".join(lines)


def between(start, end, new):
    """Replace everything from `start` up to (not including) `end`."""
    global text
    assert text.count(start) == 1 and text.count(end) == 1, (start, end)
    a, b = text.index(start), text.index(end)
    assert a < b
    text = text[:a] + new + text[b:]

    "A relation's tuples travel from the file readers",
    r'''A relation's tuples travel from the file readers to every structure's build as one `Tuples` batch (`kermit-iters/src/tuples.rs`, #111): tuples of one arity, row-major in one `Vec<usize>`, with an explicit row count, so a batch of nullary tuples keeps its count. Each row is addressed by a `RowId` (`u32`), so a batch holds at most `u32::MAX` rows. `read_csv` and `read_parquet` return one at its exact size, and the `Catalog` (see "Catalog and lifecycle") holds it untimed; the `from_tuples*` conveniences take `impl Into<Tuples>` (test fixtures pass one `Vec<usize>` per tuple, which converts). HashTrie keeps the one copy its build makes of the rows, stores row ids into it, and threads its lists through one 4-byte link per row (`ChainLinks`, `kermit-iters/src/chain_links.rs`, #101).

A structure is built from a `TupleView<'a>` (`kermit-iters/src/tuple_view.rs`): a borrowed `&Tuples`, a `Filter` and output `columns`, where output column `i` reads source column `columns[i]`. The `Filter` is closed to the two equalities a query can express, constants (`column = value`) and repeated variables (`earlier column = later column`), kept sorted so that equal filters compare equal. A view offers `matches` and `write` for one row, `for_each` and `count` over the matching rows, and the copies `materialize` (the matching rows in source order, at exact capacity), `materialize_sorted` and `gather_sorted` (sorted output rows, one copy at every arity). `TupleView::all` is the identity view; a view with no columns is legal, and its `count()` is an all-constant atom's multiplicity. Every build mode reads a view and copies the matching rows exactly once, inside the timed build: TreeTrie `serial` and ColumnTrie read `materialize_sorted()`; TreeTrie `parallel:N` tests `matches` while scattering row ids into partitions and `write`s each worker's gathered partition; HashTrie `bulk` and `incremental` take `materialize()` as the trie's buffer; and the radix family's `partition_rows` tests `matches` in its counting pass and `write`s in its scatter pass, so the partition-ordered copy is the buffer. No build allocates per input row.''',
)

# --- The query pipeline ---------------------------------------------------------------------
between(
    "### Query validation\n",
    "## Benchmarking (`kermit-bench`)\n",
    "\n\n".join(
        [
            "### Query validation",
            r'''Before anything is planned, `prepare` checks the query against the catalog's headers (`kermit/src/db/validation.rs`), in a fixed order, and returns the first failure as a `JoinError`: every head term is a variable and none repeats; each body atom names a known relation, with one term per column (constants and placeholders count); every head variable occurs in the body; and every constant is `c<digits>` (checked through `extract_accesses`). There is no check on column order: the planner is free, so `edge(X, Y), edge(Y, X)` runs over two indexes of `edge`, one per column order. There is no reserved-name check either, since access ids (`@<k>`) and index ids (`#<k>`) cannot collide with a relation name. Without these checks each malformed shape took whatever path the executors' internals allowed, and the two families diverged (issue #78) — an unbound head variable panicked in LFTJ but returned no rows from Hash Triejoin, and a wrong-arity atom returned a plausible empty result.''',
            r'''The entry points therefore never panic on a query; they return `Result<_, JoinError>`. `validate_query(query, relations)` runs the same checks without joining, against anything implementing `RelationArities` — the `Catalog`, or a slice of `RelationHeader`s read without their tuples (`kermit_ds::read_csv_header` / `read_parquet_header`). `kermit join`, `bench join` and `bench run` (through `Workload::prepare`) use the latter, so a query that cannot run exits 1 before any relation is read in full or any measurement starts.''',
            "### Placeholder rewrite",
            r'''After validation, `prepare` calls `kermit_algos::rewrite_placeholders` (see `kermit-algos/src/placeholder_rewrite.rs`), which turns every `_` in a body atom into its own fresh variable `K<i>`. Both executors assume one variable per column — the sorted iterators open one physical level per variable, and Hash Triejoin expects every iterator at its leaf once the last variable is bound — and `analyse` skips placeholders, so before the rewrite a middle `_` shifted the later columns onto the wrong level (`Q(X, Y) :- r(X, _, Y)` bound `Y` to the second column) and any `_` made Hash Triejoin panic (issue #73). After it, `_` is exactly an unused named variable, and the fresh column is dropped by the head projection.''',
            "### Access extraction",
            r'''Next, `kermit_algos::extract_accesses` (see `kermit-algos/src/access.rs`) turns each body atom into an `Access { relation, filter, columns, variables }`, column by column: a variable's first occurrence in the atom becomes a kept column, a later occurrence becomes an equality with the first (`Q(X) :- r(X, X)` keeps one column and filters `col0=col1`), and a constant `c<id>` becomes a constant filter (`col1=<id>`). Kept columns stay in source order. The result is an `AccessQuery`: the query rewritten so that body atom `i` is the access id `@i` over its kept variables, the `accesses`, and the `checks`, the atoms with no kept column (only constants). This is relational algebra's selection, applied below the join as Veldhuizen 2014 §3.4 point 4 and Freitag et al. (VLDB 2020) describe, and applied while the index is built rather than during the join, so no executor, data structure or wrapper type ever sees a constant or a repeated variable. The `Filter` is closed to those two equalities because a term is a variable, a constant or `_`. Head repeats (`Q(X, X)`) are rejected by validation, and a malformed constant is the `RewriteError` that becomes `JoinError::MalformedConstant`.''',
            "### Head projection",
            r'''The executors emit every variable of the executed query, in canonical order. `analyse` numbers the head's variables first, `0..head.len()`, and validation guarantees the head is distinct variables, so the head's columns are each row's prefix: `execute` lends the sink `&row[..head.len()]`, allocating nothing (issue #71). Body-only variables — written, or the fresh `K<i>` of a `_` — never reach the caller, and duplicates are kept, so row counts are unchanged.''',
            "### Query Planning",
            r'''After access extraction, `prepare` gathers statistics per access id and plans the join. An unfiltered access reads its relation's catalog statistics — tuple counts always, per-column distinct counts when the optimiser's `required_statistics()` asks, both gathered once from the flat data when the `Catalog` is built. A filtered access scans the flat area through its filter for exact counts (and distinct counts when asked). A planner that asks for more than the catalog holds gets `JoinError::MissingStatistics`. These statistics go into `CatalogStats`, and the `Planner` (a `QueryOptimiser` alone; there is no column-order policy) returns a `QueryPlan` — the global attribute order the algorithm will descend. Every order is valid (`Precedence::free` has no edges); provided optimisers rank candidates inside Kahn's algorithm, and `join_for_each` asserts `QueryPlan::validate` defensively. Because the statistics come from the flat data rather than a built structure, a plan no longer depends on the structure (the sorted tries counted distinct rows where HashTrie counted duplicates), and planning is untimed and happens once per query, before any timer. `LexicographicOptimiser` (default) reproduces the historical hardcoded order; `CardinalityOptimiser` prefers variables from small relations (`--optimiser cardinality`). `CostBasedOptimiser` (`--optimiser cost-based`) minimises the System R estimate of LFTJ's per-depth bindings by dynamic programming over the sets a valid plan can bind; see `docs/optimisers/cost-based.md`.''',
            "### Index planning",
            r'''Finally, `kermit_algos::plan_indexes` (see `kermit-algos/src/index_plan.rs`) turns the plan into the indexes the query builds. Each access's kept columns are sorted by the plan position of their variables, giving an `IndexSpec { relation, filter, columns }`; identical specs merge, so a self-join that reads one relation one way builds it once, while `edge(X, Y), edge(Y, X)` builds two. Specs get ids `#0`, `#1`, … in order of first appearance, and the executed query's atoms name those ids with their variables in index-column order, so by the time the plan reaches `join_for_each` every atom's term order equals its index's column order and no index is read through a wrapper. The plan is translated by variable name, since `analyse` numbers body-only variables by first appearance. The result is an `IndexPlan { query, plan, indexes }`, which `prepare` keeps, with the checks, in a `Prepared`. The step reads only the plan and the accesses, never the data, so a symmetric relation read reversed (SNAP's undirected `edge`, #96, in the 4-cycle's `edge(D, A)`) can still build a second, identical index; writing the atom `edge(A, D)` avoids it.''',
        ]
    )
    + "\n\n",
)

# --- Catalog and lifecycle ------------------------------------------------------------------
sub("### Database layer", "### Catalog and lifecycle")
line(
    "`kermit/src/db.rs` exposes one streaming join entry point",
    r'''`kermit/src/db.rs` runs a query as four steps over a `Catalog` (`kermit/src/db/catalog.rs`): the relations keyed by header name, each a header and a flat `Tuples` batch with no structure built, plus the statistics gathered once when it is built, up to the `StatisticsLevel` its optimiser declares (tuple counts are row counts; column-distinct counts only at `ColumnDistinct`). A later relation with a duplicate name replaces the earlier one.

- **Load** (untimed) reads each relation the queries name into the catalog.
- **`prepare(&catalog, &query, &planner) -> Result<Prepared, JoinError>`** (untimed, once per query; `kermit/src/db/lifecycle.rs`) validates, rewrites `_`, extracts accesses, gathers statistics, plans, and plans indexes. A `Prepared` holds the executed query, the plan, the `IndexSpec`s, the constant checks and the head's length.
- **`build::<R>(&catalog, &prepared) -> Indexes<R>`** (timed) turns each spec into a `TupleView` over its relation's flat tuples and calls the structure's `from_view`, which copies the matching rows once; each constant check becomes its view's `count()`. A zero count means the query has no answers; otherwise the counts multiply into `Indexes::multiplicity()`, each clamped to 1 unless `R::KEEPS_DUPLICATES`. `build_with` takes the constructor as a closure, which is how the binary's families inject their config and build mode.
- **`execute::<R, JA>(&prepared, &indexes, emit)`** (timed) maps ids to indexes, calls `JoinAlgo::join_for_each`, and lends `emit` each row's head prefix once per unit of multiplicity, without materialising the result; when every atom was a constant check it emits the empty head row `multiplicity` times and runs no join. Executing with indexes built from another `Prepared` is a programming error, caught by a debug assertion that the specs are equal.

The conveniences `lftj_join_for_each<R, JA>` and `hash_join_for_each<R>` (hardwired to `HashTriejoin`) run all three steps and stream; `lftj_join` / `hash_join` collect through them and return `Result<Vec<Vec<usize>>, JoinError>`; a query that cannot run returns a `JoinError` before anything is emitted. `kermit::compute_join` builds a `Catalog` from its inputs and calls them. Freeing what a timed step built is never timed: each step returns what it built, and Criterion drops it after the timer stops.''',
)
line(
    "They share a single private body.",
    r'''In the binary, `RelationFamily::build_index(header, view)` is each family's one config- and mode-aware construction site. `ExecutionFamily::build_indexes(&catalog, &prepared)` is `build_with` over it, `execute(&prepared, &indexes, sink)` runs the join, and `count_rows` counts a join's rows through `black_box`. The families hold no `Planner`, because `prepare` runs before them. `bench run` reads every relation its queries name into one `Catalog` before the loop over cells (`Workload::prepare`, which returns a `PreparedWorkload`), prepares each query once, and shares both across every cell; `bench join` (both `--output` and the benchmark) and `kermit join` go through the same `Workload::prepare`.''',
)

- **Interfaces:** none

The component pages describe the code as it stands after Stories 1 to 24, which this story only documents: no code changes. The two join-algorithm pages lose the const and selection views (a constant or a repeated variable is a filter on an index's build, so the join sees plain indexes). Each structure page says that its build reads a `TupleView` and copies the matching rows once, per build mode. The optimiser pages lose the column-order policy (the planner is free, and every index is built in plan order) and read access statistics (a filtered access is scanned once, in `prepare`). The two templates follow. Every task is edits to existing markdown pages, so each task's "failing test" is a `grep` that matches the stale text and passes once the edits are in. A few of the pages quote landmine markers (`AtomicU32`, `OnceCell`, `triejoin_open`) in text this story leaves as it is, and none of the new text adds code, so no task needs `effort: xhigh`. Line numbers in each task are those of the file at HEAD; every edit also quotes or names the text it replaces, so apply the edits last-first if you work by line number.

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement**

`docs/algorithms/leapfrog-triejoin.md`:

1. Replace line 49, the whole bullet that begins `- **Const rewrite tolerance.**`, with:

```markdown
- **Constants and repeated variables never reach the join.** `kermit::db::prepare` turns each body atom into an access (`kermit_algos::extract_accesses`, [access.rs](../../kermit-algos/src/access.rs)): a constant `c<id>` becomes a constant filter on its column, and the second and later occurrence of a variable inside one atom becomes an equality with its first. The build applies that filter while it copies the rows (`TupleView`, [tuple_view.rs](../../kermit-iters/src/tuple_view.rs)), so the join receives plain indexes, one per distinct (relation, filter, column order), whose columns are all distinct variables. LFTJ keeps the literature's one-variable-per-level assumption and no iterator wrapper stands between it and a trie. Before per-query index builds (2026-10-22), a one-value `Const_c<id>` relation and a `Select_<n>_<base>` equality view (a non-materialised `σ_{col_i = col_j}`) were wrapped around the iterators, and the view's refusal to `open` on a non-diagonal prefix was an ordinary dead prefix, handled by "A failed descent is atomic". An atom of constants only builds no index: its row count multiplies the results (`Indexes::multiplicity`), and a zero count ends the query. Regression: the `diagonal` and `repeated_nonadjacent` patterns of the standard suite, and `kermit/tests/all_orders.rs`. A new algorithm tolerates any index, since the executed query holds only `#<id>` atoms over distinct variables.
```

2. Leave line 50 (`- **Placeholders never reach the join.**`) unchanged.

3. Delete line 51 entirely, the bullet that begins `- **Repeated variables never reach the join.** The same entry point then runs`. Line 49 now carries it.

4. Replace line 52, the whole bullet that begins `- **Valid global attribute order (GAO).**`, with:

```markdown
- **Valid global attribute order (GAO).** The descent order must bind every index's variables in physical column order, because each iterator descends one stored column per `open()`. The ordering arrives as a `QueryPlan` produced by a [`QueryOptimiser`](../optimisers/) (previously it was computed in-algorithm by a now-deleted `build_variable_index`/`global_attribute_order` pair); `join_for_each` validates it with [`QueryPlan::validate`](../../kermit-algos/src/optimiser/plan.rs) and panics on an invalid plan, then permutes each result tuple back to head-first order into one scratch row (lent by `TrieIteratorWrapper::advance`, so no tuple is allocated) so output columns are independent of the descent order. The default [`LexicographicOptimiser`](../optimisers/lexicographic.md) binds the variables in canonical order. The plan can always be satisfied, because the indexes follow the plan: the planner is free, and [`plan_indexes`](../../kermit-algos/src/index_plan.rs) sorts each access's kept columns by the plan position of their variables, so every atom LFTJ sees is an index whose column order is the order the plan binds its variables in. A cyclic pair such as `r(X, Y), s(Y, X)` plans like any other query, with one of the two read through an index whose columns are swapped. A constant is no longer a variable that must be bound in a particular place: `p(c, X)` is a filter on `p`'s first column, applied when `p`'s index is built, and `kermit/tests/subject_position_constant.rs` and the LUBM cardinality test still guard it end to end. Before per-query index builds (2026-10-22), each relation's stored column order constrained the plan, a cyclic constraint set was rejected with `JoinError::CyclicAttributeOrder`, and a naive first-appearance order silently yielded 0 results for subject-position constants. The hash-trie join shares the same `QueryPlan` contract.
```

`docs/algorithms/hash-triejoin.md`:

1. Replace line 46, the whole bullet that begins `- **Singleton iterators participate normally.**`, with:

```markdown
- **Constants and repeated variables never reach the join.** `kermit::db::prepare` turns each body atom into an access (`kermit_algos::extract_accesses`): a constant is a filter on its column, and a repeated variable is an equality with its first occurrence. The build applies the filter while it copies the rows into the hash trie (`TupleView`), so every `HashTrieIterator` this algorithm sees is a real hash trie whose columns are all distinct variables, and the hash entry point takes no hash strategy `H` (it existed only to hash constants). Before per-query index builds (2026-10-22), a one-value iterator for `Const_c<id>` and a `Select_<n>_<base>` view stood in for these: the view was a one-bucket table (`size() == 1`, so `enumerate` picked it as `I_scan`) that admitted only the hash it passed at the source level and filtered its leaf chain by value. The "collision rejection is at the leaves" rule above therefore has one site again. An atom of constants only builds no index: its row count multiplies the results on a structure that keeps duplicates (`Relation::KEEPS_DUPLICATES`, true for `HashTrie`), and a zero count ends the query.
```

2. Leave line 47 (`- **Placeholders never reach the join.**`) unchanged.

3. Delete line 48 entirely, the bullet that begins `- **Repeated variables never reach the join.** The entry point also runs`.

4. In line 50, replace the exact text

```
an index into a view's own list of ids or the current row's id in a trie's chain
```

with

```

```

5. In line 57, replace the exact sentences

```
Under `--column-orders any` the plan may bind an atom's columns in any order: the orientation rewrite ([`orient`](../../kermit-algos/src/orient.rs)) reads such an atom through a reordered copy of its relation, so the term order of every atom HTJ sees still equals its hash trie's column order. Nothing in this algorithm changed for the policy.
```

with

```
The plan may bind an atom's columns in any order: [`plan_indexes`](../../kermit-algos/src/index_plan.rs) builds each atom's hash trie with its columns in plan order, so the term order of every atom HTJ sees equals its hash trie's column order, and nothing in this algorithm depends on how the relation is stored.
```

`CatalogStats::tuples(name)` per access, keyed by access id (`@0`, `@1`,

```

5. Replace lines 34 to 46 (from ``Query: `Q(A, B, C) :- R(A, B), S(A, C).` `` through the line that ends ``order `[0, 1, 2]`.``) with:

```markdown
Query: `Q(A, B, C) :- R(A, B), S(A, C).` with |R| = 1000, |S| = 3, both
unfiltered (accesses `@0` and `@1`). Canonical indices: `A = 0`,
`B = 1`, `C = 2`. No variable is constrained. Per-variable minimum sizes:
`A -> min(1000, 3) = 3`, `B -> 1000`, `C -> 3`.

1. Ready set: `{A, B, C}` with ranks 3, 1000, 3. `A` and `C` tie, and the
   canonical index breaks it. Emit `0`.
2. Ready ranks: `B = 1000`, `C = 3`. `C` wins. Emit `2`.
3. Emit `1`.

The default ordering policy: always bind the variable with the smallest
canonical index next. It is the stats-free control: the plan depends on
the query text alone. Before per-query index builds (2026-10-22) it
reproduced, bit for bit, the ordering kermit hardcoded before query
optimisers existed (`global_attribute_order`), Kahn's sort constrained by
each atom's stored column order, so benchmarks planned with it were
directly comparable with pre-optimiser measurements. Nothing is
constrained now, so the plan is the canonical order itself, and it differs
from that earlier order wherever a stored column order forced another (a
subject-position constant, a cyclic pair of atoms). Prefer it as the
control arm of optimiser ablations (e.g. against the
[cardinality optimiser](./cardinality.md)) and whenever no statistics are
available.
```

5. Replace lines 64 to 80 (everything under `## Statistics consumed`, from `` `CatalogStats::tuples(name)` and `CatalogStats::distinct(name, column)`, `` through `` and each distinct count equals the tuple count. ``) with:

```markdown
`CatalogStats::tuples(name)` and `CatalogStats::distinct(name, column)`,
for every access (keyed by access id, `@0`, `@1`, …). So it declares
`required_statistics() == StatisticsLevel::ColumnDistinct`:
- the `Catalog` counts each relation's distinct values per column once,
  when it is built (one walk per relation), outside every timer;
- `prepare` refuses to plan from less (`JoinError::MissingStatistics`);
- an unfiltered access reads its relation's catalog statistics, and a
  filtered access (a constant, or a repeated variable) is scanned through
  its filter once, in `prepare`, for exact tuple and per-column distinct
  counts, so a constant's selectivity is measured, not estimated;
- the other optimisers read only tuple counts, so their runs never pay for
  the distinct walk.

Special cases:
- A constant is a filter, not a variable: its access has fewer columns, and
  its counts are those of the rows that match.
- A repeated variable is an equality in the filter, so its counts are exact
  too (they were the base relation's, as upper bounds, while selection
  views stood in).
- Missing statistics only arise when the optimiser is called directly with
  a hand-built `CatalogStats`. The tuple count is then "assume large"
  (`usize::MAX`), and each distinct count equals the tuple count.
```

7. Replace lines 94 to 129 (the worked example, from `Query \`Q(A, B, Y) :- small(A, Y), link(c7, B), owns(B, Y).\`, rewritten to` through `pin these numbers.`) with:

````markdown
Query `Q(A, B, Y) :- small(A, Y), link(c7, B), owns(B, Y).`

**Accesses.** `prepare` reads one access per atom: `@0` is `small(A, Y)`;
`@1` is `link(c7, B)`, with the constant as the filter `col0=7`, so it
keeps only column 1, bound to B; `@2` is `owns(B, Y)`. Canonical indices:
A = 0, B = 1, Y = 2. No constraint orders the variables.

| Access | Reads | Tuples | Distinct values |
|---|---|---:|---|
| `@0` | `small(A, Y)` | 100 | A: 100, Y: 10 |
| `@1` | `link`, filter `col0=7`, column 1 | 12 | B: 12 |
| `@2` | `owns(B, Y)` | 40,000 | B: 20,000, Y: 10 |

`link` itself holds 50,000 tuples. The filtered scan found that 12 of them
have the constant in column 0, so `@1` has 12 tuples: the statistics are
those of the rows that match, not an estimate from the whole relation.

**Estimates.** For each set a plan can bind:

| S | est(S) |
|---|---:|
| {A} | 100 |
| {B} | 12 · 20,000 / 20,000 = 12 |
| {Y} | 10 · 10 / 10 = 10 |
| {A, B} | 100 · 12 · 20,000 / 20,000 = 1,200 |
| {A, Y} | 100 · 10 / 10 = 100 |
| {B, Y} | 10 · 12 · 40,000 / (20,000 · 10) = 24 |
| {A, B, Y} | 100 · 12 · 40,000 / (20,000 · 10) = 240 |

**Plans** reaching the full set:

| Plan | Cost | |
|---|---:|---|
| Y, B, A | 10 + 24 + 240 = **274** | chosen |
| B, Y, A | 12 + 24 + 240 = 276 | |
| Y, A, B | 10 + 100 + 240 = 350 | |
| B, A, Y | 12 + 1,200 + 240 = 1,452 | `cardinality`'s: the 12-tuple access binds first |
| A, B, Y | 100 + 1,200 + 240 = 1,540 | `lexicographic`'s |

`variable_ordering = [2, 1, 0]`. `plan_indexes` then builds `@0` as `small`
with columns `[1, 0]` (Y before A), `@1` as `link` with the filter
`col0=7` and columns `[1]`, and `@2` as `owns` with columns `[1, 0]` (Y
before B).

No test pins these numbers: they are this page's illustration. The unit
tests in `cost_based.rs` and `cardinality.rs` state their own constant
statistics for a similar query, and `cost_based_watdiv_plans.rs` pins the
real templates' plans (see "Index orders").
````

```markdown
### Construction

`from_view(header, view)` reads a [`TupleView`](../../kermit-iters/src/tuple_view.rs): a borrowed flat `Tuples`, a filter of constants and column equalities, and the output columns in the order the trie stores them. It copies the matching rows once, with `view.materialize_sorted()`: they come back projected, permuted and sorted lexicographically in one exact-size buffer, at every arity (up to arity 4 the copy is sorted in place; from arity 5 the ids are sorted against the view and gathered once, so no arity copies twice). `TreeTrie` then inserts each row of that buffer as a slice, and the buffer, which is scratch, is freed when the build ends. The build only reads the source, the catalog's flat area shared by every index of every query. `from_tuples(header, tuples)` is the convenience over `TupleView::all`. The header the trie holds is the relation's kept attributes in output order. Kermit-ds's tests build every mode from a filtered, permuted view and compare it with the build from that view's materialised batch.
```

## Construction

How `from_view(header, view)` reads its `TupleView`, and the one copy it makes:
- which view methods the build calls (`materialize`, `materialize_sorted`, `gather_sorted`, or `matches` and `write` while partitioning);
- what the copy is (scratch freed at the end of the build, or the structure's own buffer) and its capacity (exact: the build allocates it at the size of the matching rows);
- what each BuildMode copies, so that every mode builds an equivalent structure from the same view (the same contents and capacities, hence the same `heap_size_bytes`).

A build never moves or frees the view's source (the catalog's flat area) and allocates nothing per input row.
```

4. Lines 57 to 78 (the fenced `text` block under `### The three steps` of `## TreeTrie`, from `parallel_build(tuples, N):` through `insert each (hash, value) into root`). Replace the whole fenced block, fences included, with:

````markdown
```text
parallel_build(view, N):
    check arities                                     // the serial check, on the caller; only when the source holds rows
    if the source has no rows: return the empty trie  // no worker started
    splitters = sample of the output first keys       // the calling thread
    partitions = scatter_rows(view, morsels of 16 384, partition_of)  // step 1, N workers
        // each source row the filter keeps sends its source row id to the
        // partition whose splitters bracket its output first key
    lists = dispatch(partitions):                     // step 2, N workers
        rows = view.gather_sorted(ids)                // the one copy: this partition's rows, output order, sorted
        insert each row of rows into a local list of nodes
    trie = empty                                      // step 3, the caller
    push each partition's top-level nodes onto the root, in partition order
```
````

5. Lines 80 to 86 (the `- **Partition.**` bullet of `## TreeTrie`, from `- **Partition.** Workers take morsels from a mutex-guarded queue and push` through `thread frees the input batch once.`). Replace with:

```markdown
- **Partition.** Workers take morsels, ranges of source row ids, from a
  mutex-guarded queue and push the id of each row the filter keeps
  (`view.matches`) into its partition's bucket for that morsel; the rows
  stay in the source, which is only read. A partition is its buckets in
  morsel order, so it lists its ids in input order, strictly ascending.
  Each build worker then gathers its partition with `view.gather_sorted`:
  it sorts the ids by output row, then copies each row's output columns
  once, in that order, into a buffer of exact size, and frees the buffer
  when done. That gather is the build's one copy, inside the timer exactly
  as `serial`'s `materialize_sorted` is. Nothing frees the source.
```

```

```markdown
- **Partition.** By the top b bits of the first attribute's hash (the radix
  build's rule; FxHash mixes its low bits poorly), so there are no
  splitters to sample. Unlike TreeTrie's, this step moves the rows:
  `partition_rows` counts each morsel's matching rows per partition (a
  morsel is a range of source row ids, and `view.matches` skips the rows the
  filter rejects), then each worker copies its morsels' matching rows with
  `view.write` into disjoint ranges of one new buffer, allocated at exact
  size. Partition p is the contiguous id range `offsets[p]..offsets[p + 1]`
  of the copy, in input order, and `origin` maps each id back to its source
  row id. The source is only read.
```

## Story 27: The specs and benchmark docs

- **Developer:** junior-dev
- **Files:** `docs/specs/bench-report-schema.md`, `docs/specs/optimization-standard.md`, `docs/specs/benchmarking-architecture.md`, `docs/benchmarks/README.md`, `docs/benchmarks/H2O.md`, `docs/benchmarks/JOB.md`, `docs/benchmarks/LUBM.md`, `docs/benchmarks/SNAP.md`, `docs/benchmarks/WATDIV.md`, `BENCHMARKING.md`, `USAGE.md`, `docs/specs/space-benchmarks.md`
- **Interfaces:** none
- **Verify:** `bash -c 'grep -q -E "^\| 5 " docs/specs/bench-report-schema.md'`
- **Review:** light (documentation only; its text may quote the markers `unsafe {`, `unsafe impl`, `unsafe fn`, `AtomicU32`, `OnceCell`, `triejoin_open`, `iter_custom(`, `global_allocator`, `features = ["test-hooks"]`, `rand::`, `COPY (`, `temp_directory`, `compute_join`, `.bytes()?`, `var_name(`)

This story documents the report schema, the BuildMode standard, the benchmarking architecture and the benchmark pages as they stand after Stories 1 to 24; no code changes. `bench-report-schema.md` gains its v5 row and loses `column_orders`, `insertion` and `copies` from the current catalogue (the old rows stay as history). `optimization-standard.md` takes BuildMode equivalence from a shared `TupleView`. `benchmarking-architecture.md` takes the lifecycle (load, prepare, build, execute) and the per-query metrics. The benchmark pages drop `--column-orders` and describe per-query builds. `BENCHMARKING.md` and `USAGE.md` move to the `build` metric, schema 5 and `RelationFamily::build_index` (Task 27.5), keeping their dated statements about pre-v5 reports. `space-benchmarks.md` takes the v5 meaning of `bench run`'s `space` function and its throughput (Task 27.6). Every task is edits to existing markdown, so each task's "failing test" is a `grep` that fails on the stale text and passes once the edits are in. The new text quotes no landmine marker as code, so no task needs `effort: xhigh`. Line numbers in each task are those of the file at HEAD, and every edit also quotes or names the text it replaces; apply the edits last-first if you work by line number.

copied once in plan order, plus its all-constant checks), `iteration` (the
streamed join over indexes built once, outside Criterion; planning is
excluded, since a query is planned once, in `prepare`) and `end_to_end`
(opt-in: a build plus K joins), and one space function, `space` (the heap
bytes of the query's indexes together). `bench ds` writes `{ds}/build`,
`{ds}/iteration`, `{ds}/end_to_end` (opt-in) and `{ds}/space`. Each index
also gets an `index` metadata line, `{id} {relation} filter {filter}
columns {columns:?}: {rows} rows, {bytes} bytes`, where the filter reads
`-` for none and otherwise `col{c}={value}` for a constant and
`col{a}=col{b}` for an equality, comma-separated (for example
`#0 edge filter - columns [1, 0]: 4 rows, 96 bytes`, illustrative).

Up to v4, the time functions were `insertion` (every base relation built
from its file-order tuples), `iteration` (the streamed join over the
prebuilt engine), `end_to_end` and, under `--column-orders any` when the
plan needed a copy, `copies` (every reordered copy the query needed,
permuted and built through the same `build_relation` as `insertion`;
emitted beside `insertion`, so only when `insertion` was measured). The
space functions were `space/<relation>` per base relation and
`space/Index_<π>_<base>` per copy (e.g. `space/Index_1_0_edge`), and each
copy also got an `index` metadata line, e.g. `edge (1, 0)`. Under `stored`
no `copies` or `space/Index_*` function was ever written.
```

```markdown
## The query lifecycle

Since report schema 5, every `bench join` and `bench run` query goes through
four steps (`docs/specs/2026-10-22-per-query-index-build-design.md`):

1. **Load (untimed).** Each relation the queries name is read once into a
   `kermit::db::Catalog`: its header, its flat `Tuples` and statistics at
   the optimiser's `required_statistics()` level. No structure is built.
2. **Prepare (untimed, once per query).** `kermit::db::prepare` validates
   the query against the catalog, extracts one access per atom (relation,
   filter of constants and repeated variables, kept columns), scans
   filtered accesses for exact statistics, plans freely, and turns the
   plan into index specs (relation, filter, column order), merging
   identical ones.
3. **Build (timed).** Each spec reads the catalog's flat tuples through a
   borrowed `TupleView` and copies its rows exactly once, in the
   structure's own way (`ExecutionFamily::build_indexes`). An atom with only
   constants becomes a row count.
4. **Execute (timed).** The unchanged `JoinAlgo` runs over the plain
   indexes (`ExecutionFamily::execute`); the entry point projects to the
   head and applies the all-constant multiplicity.

Freeing what a timed step built is never timed: Criterion drops it after the
timer stops.
```

```markdown
4. Once per benchmark, before the loop over cells: `Workload::prepare`
   validates every query from the relation headers, reads every relation the
   queries name into one `Catalog` (flat `Tuples` plus statistics at the
   optimiser's `required_statistics()` level), and prepares each query once
   (access extraction, filtered statistics, free planning, index specs). No
   structure is built at load, and the result is shared by every cell.
5. For each query in the workload (filtered by `--query` if set), per
   cell: with `--verify`, run the query once and compare its count with
   `expected` (mismatch aborts; a query without `expected` is noted as not
   verified) — the count comes from `ExecutionFamily::count_rows`, which
   streams the join through a `black_box` sink and never materialises it, on
   fresh indexes when the family's joins mutate them (`JOIN_MUTATES`) — then
   run the chosen metrics. `Build`, `Iteration` and `EndToEnd` go through
   wall-clock Criterion; `Space` goes through `SpaceMeasurement`:
   - `build`: `ExecutionFamily::build_indexes(catalog, prepared)` — every
     index the query needs plus its all-constant checks — via `iter_batched`
     with a no-op setup and `BatchSize::PerIteration`: no setup copy, at most
     one set of indexes alive, freed after the timer stops;

     sink, over indexes built once outside Criterion, or, when
     `JOIN_MUTATES`, over a fresh build per sample made in untimed setup.
     Planning is excluded;
   - `end_to_end`: `build_indexes` plus K × `execute` in one timed body
     (`--queries-per-build`), which equals `build` + K × `iteration`;
   - `space`: the heap bytes of the query's indexes together, one Criterion
     function per query. A lazy HashTrie keeps the check that its footprint
     is as built.

The runner itself (`run_benchmark`, in `kermit/src/bench/run.rs`) takes a
`PreparedWorkload`, which `Workload::prepare` builds from a `Workload`, and
`Workload::from_definition` makes the `Workload`: it performs the
`ensure_cached` step and the query parsing described in step 3.

`EndToEnd` is the only metric whose timed body spans the build→query
boundary: each Criterion sample builds the query's indexes from the
catalog's flat tuples through the same call as `build`, then executes and
counts the query K times (`--queries-per-build`). `BatchSize::PerIteration`
is deliberate — batching would amortise away the per-build cost the metric
exists to measure.

2. Insert, before the line `## Cross-benchmark comparison` (line 31), this section followed by a blank line:

```markdown
## How every benchmark is run

Every benchmark here runs the same way (report schema 5). `bench run` reads each relation a query names once into a flat catalog and builds no structure at load. Each query then builds, and times as `build`, only the indexes its plan reads: an index is a relation filtered by the query's constants and repeated variables, with its columns in plan order, copied once from the catalog. A constant is therefore a filter on a build, not a view in the join. A benchmark whose queries carry constants (LUBM, WatDiv) builds smaller indexes than the whole relation; one without them (SNAP, H2O, JOB) builds each relation whole, in plan order. See [`docs/specs/2026-10-22-per-query-index-build-design.md`](../specs/2026-10-22-per-query-index-build-design.md) and [`benchmarking-architecture.md`](../specs/benchmarking-architecture.md).
```

- **Why `cycle4` is written `edge(A, D)`.** The natural last atom is `edge(D, A)`, but

  A before B before C before D, so `edge(D, A)` is `CyclicAttributeOrder`. The relation

with

```
- **Why `cycle4` is written `edge(A, D)`.** The natural last atom is `edge(D, A)`. Before
  per-query index builds (2026-10-22), the default `--column-orders stored` required every
  atom's variables to follow its stored column order, and `edge(A, B)`, `edge(B, C)`,
  `edge(C, D)` already forced A before B before C before D, so `edge(D, A)` was
  `CyclicAttributeOrder`. The relation is symmetric, so `edge(A, D)` holds the same tuples
  and the same answers; the rule is kept as written so `expected` and earlier results stay
  comparable. It also lets the indexes merge: under the plan A, B, C, D all four atoms read
  `edge` with its columns in stored order, so one index serves them. `edge(D, A)` now plans
  like any query, with a second, column-swapped index of `edge`.
```

atoms sharing an object whose subjects appear nowhere else. On such a query, every valid
plan enumerated the cross product of those subjects, under either optimiser and on every
structure. In q0264, `includes(V_v2, V_v0)` and `purchasefor(V_v7, V_v0)` share `V_v0`.

3. After the paragraph that ends `together unless you pass `allow_mixed_schema=True`.` (line 99, the v4 paragraph) and before the line `The end-to-end phase exists because`, insert this paragraph and a blank line:

```markdown
Reports with `schema_version` 5 (2026-10-22) are not comparable with v4 in
`build`, `iteration`, `end_to_end` or `space`, and have no `insertion` or
`copies` metric: `build` replaces them. Relations are read once into a flat
catalog, and each query builds, and times, only the indexes its plan reads,
once, from a borrowed view of those tuples in every build mode. So
`serial` and `bulk` builds now copy inside the timer, as `radix:K`,
`parallel:N` and `presized:N` already did; `iteration` excludes planning;
`space` is one function per query; and the `column_orders` axis is gone,
since `--column-orders` no longer exists and the planner is always free.
The v5 row of
[`docs/specs/bench-report-schema.md`](docs/specs/bench-report-schema.md)
lists the changes, and `kermit-lab` refuses to load v4 and v5 reports
together unless you pass `allow_mixed_schema=True`. There is no A/B against
v4; the first v5 measurement is the next full sweep (#99).
```
